html:
Kuru was a fatal brain disease that struck the Fore people of the Eastern Highlands of Papua New Guinea, reaching epidemic levels in the 1950s. It killed mostly women and children.

The Fore ate the bodies of dead kin as a funeral rite, and the disease spread through this practice. When the custom ended under colonial rule in the 1950s, cases slowly fell; the last known victim died in the 2000s.

Research by the American doctor Carleton Gajdusek showed it could be passed on, and won him a Nobel Prize in 1976. Kuru helped scientists understand prions, the agents behind mad cow disease. See also first contact in the Highlands and prions and mad cow disease.
